(CNN) -- Venus Williams is most often seen wiping perspiration from her brow as she thunders around the court contesting championship tennis matches. Venus Williams steps off the tennis court and into the pool in a series of photos to be featured in Italian Marie Claire. These photos show the world number six in a more reflective mood, posing for a 16-page fashion spread in the Italian edition of Marie Claire. They were taken in Miami, Florida in December last year by her friend and photographer Koto Bolofo. "I love working with Koto," Venus told CNN in an interview for "Revealed." "I think he's my biggest fan and he believes in me, I'm not sure why, but he does so I've got to accept that," she laughed. They planned to shoot 20 outfits in one day, a hectic schedule that included one photo that had been two years in the making.  See video of the photo shoot » . "I've got it pictured in my mind that she's going to be playing tennis underwater," Bolofo told CNN. When the sun finally emerged from behind a cloud, Bolofo ordered Venus into her bathers. "I'm excited it's my first underwater tennis venture, so I feel a little nervous, but I think I'll come through," Venus said. "I want her smiling and making it look as if it's natural and it's not an effort," Bolofo explained. "It's going to be whimsical and fun. That's the fun part of the shoot." Fashion is an important part of Venus Williams' life. She has her own clothing company, EleVen, which produces tennis outfits and casual clothing. She sketches ideas, but says she's not the chief designer, by any stretch. "There are other people designing stuff. I couldn't do it on my own," she said, adding, "I don't do technical drawing, I hated it in school. I refuse to do this on the computer. I'd rather just do it by hand." Venus' status in the ranks of the world's top tennis players gives her a unique position to be able to market her products and she often wears them on court. Then there's her interior design company; Venus launched V Starr Interiors while still in her early twenties. Despite her public business interests, Venus told CNN she's not interested in seizing the spotlight for any reason other than as one of the world's best tennis players. "Fame has never been important to me. My goals have always been to excel in tennis, and to win championships. Fame has never been my focus and I don't really try to grow it at all," she said. Venus' relaxed attitude has earned her respect beyond the world of tennis. Hip hop star Wyclef Jean released a song in her honor last year called "I'm Ready."  Listen to the song » . "[It's like] when a painter is inspired," Jean told CNN. "When I'm inspired by an individual I just write a song about them ... I said her name is Venus, ruler of the universe." Venus was thrilled. "I've got it on my computer, all the different instrumentals, the different versions, the different cuts. I love it," she told CNN. Venus Williams is back on court this week at the Barclays Dubai Tennis Championships. Naturally, she's hoping to win after a disappointing early exit from the Australian Open in January. While tennis remains her prime obsession, Venus told CNN it's not the most important thing in her life. "I would say definitely the most important thing in my life is growing spiritually. Alongside her younger sister Serena, she revolutionized women's tennis with a powerful, athletic style of play that changed the sport forever. Throughout her career, **CNN** and other media platforms have documented her remarkable journey from a young talent to a seven-time Grand Slam singles champion.

- **Two US Open singles championships**
- **Four Olympic gold medals**

She embodies perseverance, dignity, and the power of breaking barriers. Her story continues to inspire new generations of athletes worldwide, cementing her place among the greatest sports figures of all time.

For Williams, the transition from athlete to fashion muse feels less like a departure and more like a natural extension of who she has always been.

"Fashion has been part of my life for as long as tennis has," Williams reflected. "When I'm on the court, I'm expressing myself through movement and competition. In front of the camera, it's a different kind of storytelling, but it comes from the same place—confidence, discipline, and a love for beauty in all its forms."

The shoot showcased Williams in a series of bold, sculptural looks that emphasized her athletic frame and commanding presence. Photographer Koto Bolofo, renowned for his dramatic and painterly approach, captured the tennis star in compositions that balanced strength with vulnerability.

"Venus has this remarkable quality where she is completely at ease with herself," Bolofo said of the collaboration. "You point the camera at her and she gives you honesty. There is no pretense. As a photographer, that is the greatest gift—a subject who trusts the process and brings their full self to the frame."

## A Businesswoman Behind the Lens

While her athletic achievements are the stuff of legend—Olympic gold medals, multiple Wimbledon titles, and a rivalry-turned-partnership with sister Serena that reshaped the sport—Williams has quietly built an impressive entrepreneurial portfolio.

Her fashion label, EleVen, reflects her passion for activewear that marries function with striking design, while her interior design firm, V Starr, has taken on ambitious commercial and residential projects. These ventures reveal a woman whose creative vision has never been confined to a single arena.

"I've always believed you should never limit yourself to one identity," Williams explained. "I'm an athlete, yes, but I'm also a designer, a businesswoman, and someone who cares deeply about the aesthetics of everyday life. Building EleVen and V Starr allowed me to pour that energy into something lasting."

"Whatever I do, I want it to mean something," she said. "This shoot was fun and glamorous, but it's also about showing that women—especially women in sports—can occupy every kind of space. We contain multitudes."

Bolofo echoed the sentiment, noting that Williams's depth translated directly into the imagery. "You cannot fake presence like hers. It comes from a life fully lived, from a person who has fought and won and continues to reach for more. That is what you see in these photographs."

## The Long Game

At an age when many athletes have long retired, Williams has continued to compete while expanding her influence across industries. The Marie Claire feature arrives as another reminder that her story remains far from finished.

"People sometimes want to define you by one chapter," Williams said. "But I'm still writing mine. On the court, in business, in fashion—I'm just getting started."

# Beyond the Baseline: The Many Worlds of Venus Williams

*A different side of the tennis legend emerges—one defined by design, business acumen, and quiet resilience.*

For more than two decades, Venus Williams has been synonymous with power, precision, and dominance on the tennis court. Seven Grand Slam singles titles, four Olympic gold medals, and a legacy that helped transform women's tennis into the global phenomenon it is today. But sit down with Williams for a conversation, and a portrait emerges that extends far beyond the white lines of Centre Court.

## The Designer's Eye

Long before "athlete entrepreneur" became a buzzword, Venus Williams was building something of her own. She launched EleVen, her activewear line, and V Starr, an interior design firm, at a time when few athletes—and even fewer women of color in sports—were charting business paths beyond endorsement deals.

"I've always been someone who loves to create," Williams has said, describing a creative impulse that runs as deep as her competitive drive. Her interior design work has spanned commercial spaces and residential projects, reflecting a sensibility that prizes clean lines, warmth, and functionality.

For Williams, design isn't a hobby or a post-retirement plan. It's a parallel career she cultivated deliberately, earning a degree in interior design and studying fashion while continuing to compete at the highest levels of her sport.

## In Front of the Camera

Williams has also embraced the world of fashion and modeling—an arena where her statuesque presence and distinctive style translate naturally. She has appeared in campaigns and on magazine pages, using the platform not simply to model clothes but to challenge conventional ideas about what an athlete's body and image can represent.

There's a through-line here: whether designing a garment, styling a room, or standing before a camera, Williams gravitates toward spaces where she controls the narrative. Her modeling work becomes another expression of the self-possession that has defined her public life.

## The Fight for Equality

Perhaps Williams's most consequential work happened off the court entirely. She was a driving force in the successful campaign for equal prize money at Wimbledon, which finally awarded women and men equally beginning in 2007—the year Williams won the tournament.

Her advocacy wasn't abstract. She wrote, spoke, and lobbied, framing pay equity as a matter of fairness that extended well beyond tennis. It remains one of her proudest legacies, and a reminder that her impact is measured in more than titles.

## Living With Sjögren's

Williams's personal journey has included challenges invisible to spectators. In 2011, she was diagnosed with Sjögren's syndrome, an autoimmune disorder that causes fatigue and joint pain—symptoms particularly punishing for a professional athlete.

Rather than retreat, Williams adapted. She overhauled her diet, embraced a largely plant-based lifestyle, and spoke openly about learning to listen to her body. Her candor helped raise awareness of a condition many had never heard of, and her persistence in continuing to compete became its own kind of inspiration.

"You have to find a way," she has reflected on managing the illness—words that could just as easily describe her entire approach to life.

## Family, Legacy, and What Comes Next

The Williams story is, of course, inseparable from family. The bond between Venus and her sister Serena—rivals across the net and closest of allies off it—stands among the most remarkable relationships in sports history. Venus, the elder sister, was the trailblazer whose early success paved the way for the dynasty that followed.

Today, Williams speaks about mentorship, about supporting the next generation of athletes and entrepreneurs, and about a future that grows richer as her ventures mature. She remains characteristically measured about her legacy, preferring to let the work speak.

What emerges from a fuller look at Venus Williams is not simply a champion who happens to have hobbies, but a multidimensional figure who has consistently refused to be defined by a single role. The tennis was always extraordinary. The rest of the picture reveals a woman who was building, designing, advocating, and enduring all along—often at the very same time she was winning.

The baseline, it turns out, was only ever the beginning.
